nodes.label: Diff reading
nodes.one_line: Read an AI-generated diff line by line before accepting it, not just skim the changed file list.
know_what: Diff — the line-level change between two versions of a file, the unit that should be reviewed before any AI change is accepted
Hunk — a contiguous block of changed lines within a diff, useful for judging whether a change is as narrow as it claims to be
Unified vs side-by-side diff view — two ways of reading the same change; side-by-side often surfaces subtle reordering or logic shifts unified view hides
Semantic vs cosmetic change — a diff that alters behavior versus one that only reformats, and the need to tell which is which before skimming past it
Diff size as a review-cost signal — a diff far larger than the task implied is itself information, independent of whether any individual line looks wrong
Whitespace/formatting noise — reformatting-only changes that inflate a diff's line count and can hide a real change inside them
know_how: Read every changed hunk in a diff before accepting it, not just the files list or a change summary
Ask why a diff touches a file that wasn't part of the stated task
Separate formatting-only hunks from behavior-changing hunks mentally before judging the change
Compare the diff's size against the task's stated scope and treat a mismatch as a prompt to look closer, not a good sign of thoroughness
Read deletions as carefully as additions — a removed check or removed line is often the actual bug
habits: Never click accept on a diff without having actually read every hunk
Read the diff before reading any chat-provided summary of what it does
Pause on any file touched that wasn't named in the prompt
Treat 'the diff is large' as a reason to slow down, not a reason to skim faster
Re-read a diff a second time after a revision, since a second pass on a familiar change still catches things the first pass didn't
nodes.checkpoint: Given a 15-line diff with one subtly incorrect line hidden among correct changes, find and name the incorrect line by reading the diff alone, without running the code.
nodes.common_failure: Skimming the diff for shape (file names, roughly how many lines changed) instead of reading the actual code, so a wrong comparison operator or an inverted condition slips through because it looked structurally like the rest of the change.
sources: Google engineering practices docs — code review

nodes.label: Hallucination spotting
nodes.one_line: Recognize a hallucinated API, package, or function signature by checking it against real docs before running it.
know_what: Hallucinated API — a function, method, or package that doesn't exist but is confidently generated, often plausible because it matches a naming pattern from a real, similar API
Version mismatch — code correct for a different version of a library than the one actually installed, a frequent source of near-hallucinations
Confident wrong answer — the absence of any hedging or uncertainty marker in model output is not evidence the output is correct
Ground truth check — verifying an API call against the actual installed package's types, docs, or source, rather than against the model's own explanation of it
Plausibility bias — a hallucinated API is dangerous precisely because it looks like something that should exist, unlike an obviously wrong answer
Silent failure vs loud failure — a hallucinated API that throws immediately (safe, gets caught) versus one that silently does something adjacent to what was intended (dangerous, easy to miss)
know_how: Check any unfamiliar function or method call against the actual installed package version's docs or type definitions before trusting it
Run the code rather than just reading it whenever an API call looks unfamiliar
Treat confident, fluent explanation of an API as no evidence of its correctness
Search the installed package's source or changelog when a method's behavior seems surprising
Pin and check the exact library version in use, since a plausible-sounding call may be correct for a different version
habits: Look up any API call that isn't already familiar before running it in anything that matters
Distrust an explanation that came from the same source as the code being explained
Keep the relevant library's docs open in a tab while reviewing AI-generated calls to it
Treat a surprising or too-convenient-looking API as a prompt to verify, not a reason for relief
Note recurring hallucinated patterns (a specific package, a specific method name) so they're recognized faster next time

know_why.claim: A model's fluency and confidence carry no information about whether an API call is real.
know_why.because: Language models generate the most statistically plausible continuation, and a plausible-sounding function name from a familiar naming pattern is exactly as fluent whether or not it exists — fluency measures training-data pattern match, not ground truth.
know_why.disputed_by: Some agentic-autonomy practitioners argue that as long as the code is run and its output verified immediately, rather than trusted from reading alone, the confidence question is moot — verification happens at execution, not at read time.
know_why.source: Practitioner writing on LLM hallucination in code generation (industry blog posts on AI-assisted development pitfalls)

nodes.checkpoint: Given five AI-generated function calls, three real and two plausible-sounding but nonexistent, correctly identify the two hallucinated calls by checking them against actual documentation.
nodes.common_failure: Trusting a hallucinated API because the surrounding code and the explanation of it both read fluently — fluency is not correctness, and a hallucinated call often only fails at runtime, or worse, silently returns something adjacent to what was expected.
sources: Package documentation / type definitions (ground truth, not the model)
industry writing on LLM code hallucination

nodes.label: Manual smoke test
nodes.one_line: Run the actual feature by hand after an AI change instead of trusting that it compiled.
know_what: Smoke test — running the actual feature by hand through its main path, the minimum bar before trusting any change, AI-written or not
Compiles-but-wrong — code that type-checks and builds cleanly while still being behaviorally incorrect, the specific gap a smoke test closes
Happy-path smoke test — exercising the primary intended flow, the minimum useful smoke test even when it isn't exhaustive
Environment parity — running the smoke test in an environment close enough to real usage (real data shape, real browser) that it would actually catch a real bug
Click-through vs automated smoke test — a quick manual pass for immediate feedback versus a scripted one for repeatability; both have a place, neither replaces the other early on
know_how: Run the exact feature just changed, by hand, before considering a change done
Use realistic input, not just the first value that comes to mind, when exercising the change
Check the browser console or terminal output during the smoke test, not just the visible UI
Test the change in the environment it will actually run in, not only in an idealized local setup
Repeat the smoke test after any further AI revision, since a later fix can silently reintroduce an earlier bug
habits: Treat 'it compiled' and 'it works' as two separate claims, never conflate them
Run the feature by hand immediately after any AI change, before moving to the next task
Watch for errors in the console during a smoke test, not just watch the screen
Re-run the smoke test after each subsequent revision, not just the first version
Smoke-test the exact scenario from the original bug report or spec, not just something nearby
nodes.checkpoint: Given an AI-generated change that compiles cleanly, manually exercise its actual behavior and correctly identify whether it does what the task asked, in under five minutes.
nodes.common_failure: Treating a clean build or a passing type check as proof the feature works — many real bugs (wrong data displayed, a handler that doesn't fire, an off-by-one in a loop) are invisible to the compiler and only show up when the feature is actually run.

nodes.label: Unit test generation
nodes.one_line: Have an assistant write tests for the behavior it just implemented, then check the tests actually assert the right thing.
know_what: Generated test — a test an AI writes for code it (or a person) just implemented, useful but only as good as its assertions
Tautological test — a test that asserts the implementation does what the implementation does, rather than what the spec requires, a common AI-generated failure mode
Assertion strength — the difference between a test that checks a real property (a computed total is correct) and one that only checks a function didn't throw
Coverage vs correctness — a test suite covering every line without checking a single behavior correctly, versus fewer tests that check the behaviors that matter
Test-writes-to-pass risk — an AI generating both the implementation and its test in the same session, so a shared misunderstanding shows up in both and the test passes despite the bug
know_how: Read every generated assertion and confirm it checks the actual requirement, not just that code ran without error
Ask explicitly for edge-case tests (empty input, boundary values, error paths), since a first pass usually covers only the happy path
Have a different session or a human write the test when the same session wrote the implementation, to avoid a shared blind spot
Break a test on purpose (comment out the real logic) to confirm it actually fails when the implementation is wrong
Reject a test that only asserts 'no exception was thrown' as insufficient
habits: Read generated test assertions line by line, not just check that the test file exists
Deliberately break the implementation once to confirm each new test actually catches it
Ask for edge-case tests explicitly rather than assuming the first pass covered them
Treat a suspiciously easy 100% pass rate on a first generated suite as a reason to check the assertions, not a reason for confidence
Keep tests and implementation reviewed as a pair, not the test accepted just because it's green
nodes.checkpoint: Given an AI-generated function and an AI-generated test suite for it, find at least one assertion that would still pass even if the function had a real bug, by deliberately breaking the implementation.
nodes.common_failure: Accepting a generated test suite because it's green — a test that only asserts a function returns 'something' or doesn't throw will pass against a badly broken implementation just as easily as a correct one.

nodes.label: Type-checking gate
nodes.one_line: Run the type checker after every AI edit and treat a type error as a required gate, not a suggestion to ignore.
know_what: Type checker — a tool (TypeScript, mypy, Flow) that verifies a program's types are internally consistent without running it, catching a specific class of bug for free
any/unknown escape hatch — a type annotation that opts out of checking, which an AI will reach for under pressure to make an error go away rather than fix the real mismatch
Structural vs nominal typing — how two types are judged compatible, relevant because AI-generated code sometimes produces a type that's structurally close but not the type actually expected
Type error as gate, not suggestion — the practice of treating any type error as blocking, rather than something to silence with a cast or an ignore comment
Strict mode — a type checker's stricter setting (TypeScript strict, mypy --strict) that catches more classes of error, often not on by default in an AI-scaffolded project
know_how: Run the type checker after every AI-generated change, as a standing step, not an occasional one
Read a type error's actual message before asking the assistant to fix it, so the fix addresses the real mismatch
Reject a fix that resolves a type error by adding any, unknown, or an as cast without justification
Turn on strict mode early in a project rather than retrofitting it once errors have accumulated
Treat a type error surfaced after a change as a signal the change's assumptions were wrong somewhere, not just a formality to clear
habits: Run the type checker before manually testing anything, since it's faster and catches a distinct class of bug
Read every type error message in full before accepting a proposed fix for it
Flag any fix that silences a type error with a cast or ignore comment instead of resolving the mismatch
Keep strict mode on and treat a request to loosen it as something to question, not to grant by default
Re-run the type checker after every subsequent revision, not just the first pass
nodes.checkpoint: Given an AI-generated change that introduces a type error, get a fix that resolves the actual type mismatch — not one that silences the error with any, an ignore comment, or an unjustified cast.
nodes.common_failure: Accepting a fix that makes a type error disappear by weakening the type (adding any or an unchecked cast) instead of correcting the underlying mismatch — the error is gone but the bug the type checker was trying to catch is still there.

nodes.label: Regression check
nodes.one_line: Run the existing test suite after an AI change to catch regressions the AI's own tests wouldn't reveal.
know_what: Regression — a previously working behavior that breaks as a side effect of an unrelated change, the specific risk a full test-suite run is meant to catch
Existing test suite as a second opinion — running tests the current session didn't write, so a shared blind spot in one session's work doesn't go unchecked
Flaky test — a test that fails intermittently for reasons unrelated to the change, which must be told apart from a real regression before either is dismissed
Blast radius of a change — which parts of the existing suite are even plausibly affected by a given change, useful for prioritizing where to look first at a failure
Full run vs targeted run — running the whole suite versus only the tests near the change, a tradeoff between speed and the chance of missing a distant regression
know_how: Run the full existing test suite after any AI change, not just the tests related to the change
Investigate every new failure individually rather than re-running until it happens to pass
Distinguish a genuinely flaky test (fails intermittently regardless of the change) from a real regression before dismissing a failure
Bisect a change into smaller pieces when a regression's cause isn't obvious from the diff alone
Re-run the full suite one more time after a regression fix, since a fix can introduce a second regression
habits: Never skip the full suite run because the change 'seems unrelated' to most of the code it covers
Treat a new failure as guilty until proven flaky, not the other way around
Keep a short list of known-flaky tests so a real regression doesn't get mistaken for one of them
Re-run the whole suite after a regression fix, not just the test that was failing
Log which change caused a regression once found, so the same class of side effect is easier to spot next time
nodes.checkpoint: Given a passing test suite and an AI-generated change unrelated to a specific existing test, run the suite, find the test that now fails, and correctly determine whether it's a real regression or a flaky test.
nodes.common_failure: Running only the tests that seem related to the change, missing a regression in a distant part of the codebase that depended on behavior the change altered incidentally — the exact case a full-suite run exists to catch.

nodes.label: Review checklist
nodes.one_line: Apply a fixed checklist — security, error handling, edge cases — to AI-generated code the way you'd review a junior engineer's pull request.
know_what: Review checklist — a fixed, written set of checks (security, error handling, edge cases, resource cleanup) applied to every AI-generated change regardless of how confident it looks

Confidence-blindness — the fact that AI-generated code's fluency doesn't correlate with its risk, so a checklist that runs regardless of how 'obviously fine' something looks catches what confidence-based review misses

OWASP-class issues — injection, broken auth, sensitive data exposure — categories worth a standing checklist item since AI-generated code reproduces insecure patterns from training data as readily as secure ones
Resource cleanup — closing connections, clearing timers, unsubscribing listeners, a category of bug AI-generated code omits because the happy path doesn't need it to 'work'
Checklist fatigue — a checklist so long or generic it stops getting read carefully, the specific failure mode a good checklist must be designed to avoid
know_how: Apply the same fixed checklist to every AI-generated change of a given type (endpoint, component, migration), not a different ad hoc review each time
Check for injection and auth bypass explicitly on any change that touches user input or access control
Check for resource cleanup explicitly on any change that opens a connection, timer, or subscription
Keep the checklist short enough to actually run every time, adding an item only when a real past bug justifies it
Treat a checklist pass as necessary, not sufficient — it catches known categories, not everything
habits: Run the checklist even on a change that 'looks obviously fine'
Update the checklist after any bug that slipped through, so the same category is caught next time
Resist checklist bloat by removing an item that hasn't caught a real bug in a long stretch
Apply the checklist consistently across changes rather than only on ones that feel risky
Read the checklist itself periodically for staleness, not just apply it mechanically forever

know_why.claim: A fixed checklist should be applied uniformly, even to changes that feel safe.
know_why.because: Confidence in a change's safety is generated by the same fluency that makes hallucinations convincing, so 'this one looks fine' is not a signal that correlates with actual risk — the checklist exists precisely to substitute a mechanical check for that unreliable feeling.
know_why.disputed_by: The vibe-loop and agentic-autonomy schools argue a uniform checklist on every change is exactly the ceremony that kills iteration speed, and prefer reserving deep checklist review for changes that touch auth, money, or data deletion, trusting lighter review elsewhere.
know_why.source: Software review practice literature (Google engineering practices docs); practitioner debate on AI-assisted review overhead

nodes.checkpoint: Given an AI-generated endpoint that looks correct on read-through, apply a fixed security/error-handling/cleanup checklist and find at least one real issue a confidence-based read alone would have missed.
nodes.common_failure: Reviewing AI-generated code only as carefully as it 'feels' like it needs, so a fluent, confident-looking change that happens to contain a real security or resource-leak issue gets the same light pass as something genuinely simple.
sources: Google engineering practices docs — code review
